newsitem.title: JAPAN: Big bankruptcies continue to hurt corporate Japan.
newsitem.headline: Big bankruptcies continue to hurt corporate Japan.

text.p: Japan's feeble economic recovery continues to mean a high level of business failures for Japanese companies, a leading research firm said Monday.

Total debts held by Japanese firms that went bust last month nearly tripled, bringing the bankruptcy debt for the full 1996/97 financial year to a record 9.26 trillion yen ($73.4 billion), Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd said.
"A high number of companies went insolvent due to the prolonged sluggish economy in March," it said in its report.
Total debts held by bankrupt firms in March surged 180.9 percent from a year earlier to 1.42 trillion yen ($11.2 billion). The figure was up 91.3 percent from February, it said.
The number of bankruptcies in March rose 2 percent from a year earlier to 1,373. It was up 12 percent from February.
About 60 percent of bankruptcies in March resulted from factors that the research firm said were typical in a slow economy -- sluggish sales, accumulated losses and unpaid bills.
The number of large-scale bankruptcies, or those with debts of more than one billion yen ($7.9 million), hit 94 in March, the third-largest number ever for a single month, it said.
Of the 94, 13 firms had debts of more than 10 billion yen ($79.3 million).
In March, finance and real estate companies went under with massive debts, boosting the total bankruptcy debt for the month and the year.

A rising number of firms in the financial and property sectors went insolvent due to aggressive investment during Japan's "bubble" era of inflated stock and land prices in late 1980s, industry analysts said.
The previous record debt level for the year was 8.63 trillion yen ($68.4 billion at current exchange rates) in 1995/96.

Among the firms that went bust in the year were financing company Nichiei Finance Co. Ltd, which became the first Japanese firm on record to fail with debts of more than one trillion yen ($7.9 billion).
Tokyo Shoko said the number of bankruptcies has risen for three successive months since January, casting doubt over the Japanese government's assessment that the economy is gradually recovering.
"Many people say that such views do not correctly present the reality of the economy," it said.

"Some listed companies failed at the beginning of this year and worries about the health of banks are rising. The signs are becoming clearer that an increasing number of medium-sized firms are going bankrupt," it said.

Tokyo Shoko expects bankruptcies to increase in the future as Japan proceeds with its financial and economic deregulation and continues to deal with bad assets from the bursting of the bubble economy.

There are also other worrisome factors, including the yen's fall, a higher rate of consumption tax and a widening gap between Japanese and U.S. interest rates, which may hurt the Japanese economy, Tokyo Shoko said.
